source: JZ Mock B · Paper 2 · Question 11 · Publisher worked answer
label: JZ Mock B · Paper 2 · Question 11
knowledgePattern: Separate a divisibility criterion from its weaker necessary condition
solution:
Try a few small values: for n=1,2,3,4, the expression n3+5n gives 6,18,42,84. The value n=4 works, so a necessary condition must hold when n=4.

Now check whether an odd n could work. Write n=2m+1. Then n3+5n=n(n2+5)=2(2m+1)(2m2+2m+3). Both brackets are odd, so the expression has only one factor of 2. A multiple of 12 needs at least two, so no odd n can work.

Every successful n is therefore even: this condition is necessary. It is not sufficient, because n=2 is even but gives 18, which is not divisible by 12.

Hence the answer is C. The small-value table suggested the pattern; the odd-integer calculation proved the necessary direction.

hints.title: Try a few small integers
hints.body: Calculate n³+5n for n=1,2,3,4. Mark which results are divisible by 12.
hints.recap: Examples can rule out conditions and suggest what to prove.
hints.pitfall: A few successes do not prove a necessary condition.
hints.pause: Compare your table with each possible condition.

recall.reminder: Necessary means every successful n must satisfy the condition.

hints.title: Test the odd case properly
hints.body: Write an odd integer as n=2m+1. Substitute into n(n2+5), and count the factors of 2.
hints.recap: A multiple of 12 must contain at least two factors of 2.
hints.pitfall: To show a condition is not sufficient, you also need a value satisfying it that fails the divisibility test.
hints.pause: Prove what happens for odd n, then test the reverse implication with your small-value table.

recall.reminder: Use integer cases to prove a divisibility claim for all integers.
